File names are bytes, not strings, but paths and ref names cross the FFI back to the core as UTF-8 only. Non-UTF-8 names display with replacement characters, and a file with one is still reachable by object id in tree browsing. By path it is not: blame, path history, worktree reads and guard actions would resolve the U+FFFD spelling, which can name a different object. So the app refuses blame, file history, Copy Path and reveal on such a path, leaves such a status row out of commit, stash and discard, and offers no delete or create on such a ref.
Blob reads and diffs are capped. The header is checked before decoding; the default cap is 8 MiB, the core clamps any cap to 4 GiB (
, applied inside every read that takes one, so every caller gets it), and the app refuses "Load anyway" above 512 MiB.
Binary detection follows git: a NUL in the first 8000 bytes. Binary content is never handed to the text view.
Errors are messages, never panics. Clippy denies
outside tests; release builds abort on panic rather than unwind across the C boundary.

is accepted for loopback hosts, so tests can run a local server end to end), and sends credentials only when the caller passed them. SSH host keys are verified against a read-only

: an unknown key is refused until the user approves its fingerprint, and a contradicting key is always fatal. A key that contradicts an approval made in the app is fatal too; the only way past it is for the user to remove that host's approval in Settings, after which the next fetch treats the key as unknown and asks again. The app never drops an approval on its own. Nothing else in a repository operation leaves the machine; the updater below is the one exception.

the app can signal from another thread; the step in flight notices it within 200 ms. The ssh transport wakes out of its connect and every read to look at it, and abandons a host-name lookup it no longer needs rather than waiting for the resolver. curl has no interrupt, so every HTTPS network step (connect, handshake, pack receive, upload, report read) runs on a detached thread the call stops waiting for; that thread lingers until its next object or 64 KiB upload chunk, or until curl's timeout below ends it. The pack steps check the flag between objects. A connection that stops moving bytes dies on its own after 120 seconds —

set in code for curl (an isolated open reads no global config), an idle budget per read and write for ssh — with one 30-second budget that dialing, the handshake, authentication and, for ssh, opening the session channel share. A cancelled operation stops between steps: nothing is left half-applied. A transfer already past its last check can still land after the cancel returns — a fetch moving its tracking refs, a push the server accepts — exactly as if it had finished just before; the next fetch shows it. A fetch claims its repository until its thread really ends, so a fetch started right after a cancelled one waits for it (up to the connect budget) instead of racing its ref updates, and otherwise refuses with a retry message. The last cancel check before gix moves the tracking refs is just before the pack receive; past it, only the pack writer's per-object check can still stop the fetch.
